**The big idea:** students find out how fast the computer really is. A benchmark is just a loop with a stopwatch around it, so this is where loops become the main event: counting, adding, building strings, testing primes, and repeating until time runs out. Students run the same benchmark on the classroom computer, in the browser, and on Google Colab, and explain the difference. They also test themselves against the computer with a reaction timer and a typing test.

**Why students care:** students compare phones, laptops, and gaming PCs all the time. Here they build the tool that settles the argument, and learn why "faster" depends on what you measure.

**Expectations:** A2.2, A2.3, A3.1, A3.2, A4.1, A4.4, B1.1, B2.1, B2.4, B3.2, B4.5, C1.2, C1.4

## Anchor Programs

- **Count to a million:** `time.perf_counter()` around a `for` loop.
- **Benchmark suite:** several short tests (counting, building a long string, checking for primes), so "fast" is measured more than one way. (Determination of primes, B3.2.)
- **Reaction timer:** wait a random time, say "GO!", and measure how fast the user presses Enter.
- **Is shuffle really random?** Shuffle a playlist 1000 times and count how often each song plays first, to answer the common complaint that shuffle "keeps playing the same songs".
- **Typing speed test:** words per minute and accuracy.

## Planned Lessons

| Lesson | Focus | Students read, then build |
|---|---|---|
| 1. How Fast Is This Computer? | Reading a benchmark; `for` and `range()`; the `time` module (A3.1) | Time counting to one million, then ten million |
| 2. Counting and Adding | Counters and accumulators; comparing a loop to a formula (B3.2) | Add 1 to *n* with a loop and with *n*(*n*+1)/2; which is faster? |
| 3. A Fair Benchmark Suite | Nested loops and decisions; checking for primes as one test among several (A2.3, B3.2); fair tests: repeat and take the median (B1.1); reading and modifying a three-test benchmark suite | Make: the **Download Time Table** Quick Build |
| 4. Run It Everywhere | Same code, different machines; CPU type and cores (C1.2, C1.4) | Compare results from the classroom, the browser, and Colab |
| 5. Keep Going Until… | `while` loops; loop conditions; infinite loops and how to stop them | Make: the **Study Timer** Quick Build (25 minutes on, 5 off); modify the benchmark to run until five seconds pass |
| 6. Reaction Timer | `random`, `time`, and `input()` together | A reaction test; best of five |
| 7. Is Shuffle Really Random? | Simulation; `random.shuffle()`; counting results (reading and modifying a list of counts) | 1000 shuffles, with a simple text bar chart |
| 8. Plan It, Then Wrap It | Flow charts and pseudocode (B2.4); working from a skeleton (B2.1); reading and modifying `def`, parameters, and return values (A3.2) | A flow chart for the typing test; wrap the benchmark in a `time_it()` function |
| 9. Debugging a Loop | Tracing; printing variables to find a bug; off-by-one errors (A4.1, A4.4, B4.5) | Fix three broken benchmarks |
| 10. Review and assignment work period | A short review of Lessons 1–9, then class time for the assignment | Finish the Typing Speed Test |
| 11. Module 3 test | Code reading and tracing; a short basics section | |

## Assignment (Planned): Typing Speed Test

From a teacher-supplied skeleton, students build a typing test that shows a sentence, times the user, and reports words per minute and accuracy. They plan it first with a **flow chart**, then hand in the program and a short **benchmark report**: their benchmark suite run on at least two different computers, with an explanation of the results.

**Adds to the toolkit:** `benchmark.py`: the benchmark suite as functions, reused in Module 4's crack-time estimate.

## Practising the Basics (Planned)

- **Skill Builder:** `for` and `range()`, `while`, counters and accumulators, nested loops, and tracing loops in a table. Includes Module 2 decisions and conversions.
- **Quick Builds** (small graded programs; each is the Make product of a lesson, so it needs no extra period):
  - **Download Time Table** (Lesson 3): a table of how long files of different sizes take to download at different speeds (nested loops, aligned columns).
  - **Study Timer** (Lesson 5): a countdown with work and break periods and a session count.
- **Warm-ups** in every lesson include a question from an earlier module.

## Notes for Teachers

- **This is where loops are written, not just read.** Students met `for` in Module 1 and modified one in Module 2.
- **Fair tests:** close other programs, run each benchmark three times, and take the median. This is good science and good problem solving.
- **Browser timings** are slower and vary more. That's the point of Lesson 4.
